title: A Composability Analysis Framework for Web3 Wallet Recovery Mechanisms
abstract: Modern Web3 wallets offer hybrid recovery solutions that combine multiple key recovery methods to balance security, availability, and usability. These methods include secret sharing of wallet private keys, encrypted cloud storage, and smart contract-based advanced recovery functionalities. However, such combined approaches can introduce new attack vectors that are not present in standalone recovery solutions. In this work, we propose a formal security analysis framework for blockchain/Web3 wallet designs with key or asset recovery functionalities. To assess whether a wallet design is secure, our framework considers several factors, including user availability and responsiveness to malicious actions, cocustodianship with external parties, the total value of assets managed by the wallet, and the reputation of the entities chosen by the user to facilitate spending or recovery functionalities. Through probabilistic model checking, our framework identifies the conditions under which a wallet design remains secure. We also include two examples of Web3 wallet designs with composite recovery mechanisms (inspired by existing designs) to demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

Modern Web3 wallets offer hybrid recovery solu- tions that combine multiple key recovery methods to balance security, availability, and usability. These methods include secret sharing of wallet private keys, encrypted cloud storage, and smart contract-based advanced recovery functionalities. However, such combined approaches can introduce new attack vectors that are not present in standalone recovery solutions. In this work, we propose a formal security analysis frame- work for blockchain/Web3 wallet designs with key or asset recovery functionalities. To assess whether a wallet design is secure, our framework considers several factors, including user availability and responsiveness to malicious actions, co- custodianship with external parties, the total value of assets managed by the wallet, and the reputation of the entities chosen by the user to facilitate spending or recovery functionalities. Through probabilistic model checking, our framework identi- fies the conditions under which a wallet design remains secure. We also include two examples of Web3 wallet designs with composite recovery mechanisms (inspired by existing designs) to demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. 1. Introduction Traditional banking systems ensure account identifica- tion, theft insurance, and the ability to revoke and renew account access credentials. However, these protections are not applicable in decentralized cryptocurrency ecosystems, where Web3 wallets are solely governed by cryptographic keys. In the event of key loss or theft, users face an immedi- ate and often irreversible loss of access to their funds, with no centralized entity able to intervene. To mitigate these risks, various wallet recovery approaches have emerged, such as multi-party computation (MPC), threshold signa- tures, and multi-signature schemes. Although these methods improve key security, they often do so at the expense of availability and usability, increasing complexity, and some- times broadening the wallet's attack surface [15]. These challenges extend beyond personal cryptocurrency wallets to organizational wallets that secure client assets on public blockchains. In response, more flexible recovery mechanisms have been developed in recent years to address key loss scenarios [15]. Some solutions employ advanced protocols and programmable logic through smart contracts, distributing recovery shares across multiple locations or storing encrypted keys on secure servers [9], [26]. To give users more recovery options while balancing security, availability, and usability, certain web3 wallets [1], [5] now combine multiple recovery methods. For instance, some wallets allow recovery using an encrypted key stored with a recovery agent, with the encryption key held in the user's personal cloud storage. Alternatively, recovery can occur through a “key rotation” process using a smart con- tract that can be initiated by user-designated entities (often called “guardians”). However, as discussed later, composing different recovery methods can introduce new attack vectors that may not exist in standalone recovery solutions. Consider a simple example of a wallet design where a single recovery agent manages two distinct recovery meth- ods: sending the encrypted key back to the user and facili- tating smart contract-based recovery. If this agent becomes aware that the user has lost the private key, such as through an encrypted key request, it could exploit this information. Rather than returning the encrypted key, the agent could initiate an “unauthorized” recovery via the smart contract, transferring account ownership to a key it controls and effectively taking over the user's account and assets. In typical scenarios, such an unauthorized recovery at- tempt would carry substantial risk for the agent, as the user, if still in possession of the private key, could issue a challenge to revert ownership. However, in this case, the agent's “side-channel” knowledge-that the user has lost the key-significantly increases its incentive to attempt this attack, now with a high probability of success. Lacking any effective means to defend against this exploitation, the user would be left vulnerable to an adversarial agent with privileged knowledge and control over multiple recovery methods. Our contributions. In this paper, we introduce a novel security analysis framework that can be applied to any self-custodial or non-custodial web3 wallet design featuring recovery functionalities. Our framework demonstrates that wallet security is dynamic and influenced by a variety of parameters. Core parameters include the asset value held in the wallet, the reputation of the wallet agents, and the probability of the user responding to malicious actions within a specific timeframe. Additional parameters may also be relevant depending on the wallet design, such as the 1531 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00158 spending power assigned to external agents and the time delays within smart contract-based recovery protocols. Using these parameters, our framework models wallet security as a game between an adversary, attempting to corrupt wallet agents, and the user. The adversary's goal is to maximize its expected gains, while the framework considers a wallet design secure if a rational adversary's optimal strategy is to follow the protocol even when agents are compromised. Through model-checking experiments, we demonstrate that our framework effectively evaluates wallet security in complex, multi-agent recovery designs. Additionally, our analysis, using both model checking and machine learning techniques, highlights the relative impact of various parameters, offering valuable insights into how these factors collectively influence wallet security. Limitations. Our framework eventually serves as a proactive method to indicate the conditions under which a given wallet design can become insecure in the presence of a rational adversary. Although blockchains naturally offer rich historical data that could be used retroactively to validate our framework's results, the absence of publicly disclosed data with attacks from malicious agents makes such an analysis infeasible. We discuss this further in Section 6.2. In addition, we only consider rational adversaries in our threat model which are strategically motivated by profit. Although attackers with non-monetary incentives might exist, their behavior is unpredictable and difficult to model without empirical data. Regardless, our goal is not to prevent every possible attack, but to provide users with a tool to make informed decisions that help avoid profitable attacks under a rational adversary model. Finally, as discussed in our contri- butions paragraph, our framework applies to self-custodial and non-custodial wallets. Custodial wallets, in which the cryptographic secrets are fully controlled by a centralized organization on behalf of the user(s), are out of scope. This exclusion also extends to certain “hybrid” approaches-such as Ava's Core wallet [18]-which provide non-custodial signing-as-a-service functionality but introduce custodial- like dependencies. Paper organization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we provide the necessary definitions and background used in the paper. In Section 3 we provide an initial overview of our framework. In Section 4 we provide the main description of the model used by our framework. In Section 5 we present two wallet designs with composed recovery functionalities as examples, and show how our framework is applied in those. In Section 6 we discuss how the model checking formal verification method can be subsequently applied to the model output to systematize the detection of strategies where an adversary would corrupt agents to increase its end value (and therefore making the wallet design insecure). In Section 7 we discuss related works. We conclude in Section 8. 2. Preliminaries 2.1. Cryptographic primitives Notation. We denote by [a] a list of an arbitrary number of elements a1, a2, ... and by min([a]) the element with the smallest value in the list. We provide informal background for the primitives we use in our paper below. Secret sharing. A Threshold Secret Sharing (TSS) scheme [19] is a cryptographic method to distribute shares of a secret among n parties. In this scheme, any subset of t + 1 or more parties can collaborate to reconstruct the secret, while any subset of t or fewer parties cannot deduce any information about the secret. This ensures both the confidentiality and the robustness of the secret. Typically, Shamir's Secret Sharing [35] is a common implementation of this scheme, where polynomial interpolation is used to achieve the desired properties. Threshold signatures and multi-signatures. A threshold signature scheme [36], [10] enables a set of parties to generate partial threshold signatures such that the aggre- gated signature, formed from any t + 1 or more partial signatures, can be verified using the group public key. The secret key required for signature generation is distributed among the set of parties creating the threshold signature. While this method is designed to enhance security and fault tolerance in theory-by preventing a single point of failure since the secret key is never fully reconstructed at any single location-in practice, implementing threshold signa- ture schemes can be complex and may not always provide the anticipated security benefits except in certain cases like BLS signatures [11]. Similarly, in a multi-signature scheme [10], [25], each of the n parties possesses an independent key pair and generates an independent signature. Signatures for a given message together form a multi-signature. Since any threshold access structure can be realized using multi- signatures in a similar fashion to threshold signatures, we use them interchangeably for the purposes of our paper. 2.2. Recovery methods in Web3 wallets This section reviews prominent methods for account and key recovery in Web3 wallets. We exclude legacy methods, such as duplicating private keys across devices, using paper wallets, QR codes, or seed phrases [32], as these either increase the attack surface significantly or further complicate key management for the average user [15]. Secret shared/encrypted keys. In this method, key data is distributed across multiple servers, allowing it to be reconstructed when needed (e.g. after a user's private key is lost). A critical assumption is that the servers do not collude, ensuring that an adversary cannot compromise more than one server. A common approach used by Web3 wal- lets [1] is to encrypt the private key with a “Key Encryption Key” (KEK), storing the KEK and encrypted private key 1532
